core: U.S. federal and state constitutional foundations

claims.claim: Article VI identifies the U.S. Constitution, federal laws made pursuant to it, and treaties made under U.S. authority as the supreme law of the land and binds state judges despite contrary state law.
The CFR is the codification of general and permanent rules published in the Federal Register by federal departments and agencies and is organized by titles, chapters, parts, and sections.
A statute is law enacted by a legislature.
Common law develops through judicial decisions rather than enacted statutes, and legislatures may codify, modify, or replace common-law rules.
In federal administrative law, a rule's source and legal effect depend on context; interpretive rules and policy statements can differ from legislative rules.
Administrative agencies act within constitutional and statutory parameters, while guidance actions can explain an agency stance without having the force of law.
The eCFR is an updated editorial compilation rather than an official legal edition of the CFR.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive, source-supported account of legal-source types, legal authority, or jurisdiction.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with a jurisdiction-qualified U.S. source map.
Added a distinction between binding regulations and agency guidance.

rightsIssues: All sources are used as reference-only. The lesson contains original explanatory prose and no reproduced statutory, regulatory, or source text beyond short source names.

sourceRecords.title: The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration
sourceRecords.notes: Read the official transcript. Supports the Article I allocation of federal legislative power, Article III judicial power, and Article VI Supremacy Clause. Used to state the federal constitutional framework and its qualified conflict rule; no constitutional prose was reproduced in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Code of Federal Regulations
sourceRecords.notes: Read the official GovInfo overview. Supports the description of the CFR as the codification of general and permanent rules published in the Federal Register by federal departments and agencies; its title/chapter/part/section organization; and the explanation that the eCFR is an unofficial editorial compilation updated daily.

sourceRecords.title: statute | Wex | US Law
sourceRecords.provider: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read the LII Wex entry as an accessible legal-definition cross-check. Supports the general definition of statute as enacted legislation; original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: common law | Wex | US Law
sourceRecords.provider: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read the LII Wex entry. Supports the distinction between law developed through judicial decisions and statutes, the role of precedent, the primarily state-level character of common law, and the ability of legislatures to codify or replace common-law rules.

sourceRecords.title: rule | Wex | US Law
sourceRecords.provider: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read the LII Wex entry. Supports that a rule's source and legal effect are context dependent; that a federal legislative rule can have force and effect of law when issued under delegated authority; and that interpretive rules and policy statements may have a different legal effect.

sourceRecords.title: administrative law | Wex | US Law
sourceRecords.provider: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read the LII Wex entry. Supports the high-level account that agencies are created and constrained by statutes and constitutional parameters, make and administer rules, and can issue interpretive guidance that does not have the force of law. The lesson avoids case-specific deference doctrine.
